query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing approximately 1 atomic percent of carbon into a phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloy (e.g., Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20) during melt processing and rapid cooling will suppress crystal nucleation, thereby improving the glass-forming ability and expanding the supercooled liquid region by at least ~20 K compared to the undoped alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A molten, phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloy in composition similar to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
generation.intervention: Addition of a controlled minor dopant of carbon (approximately 1 at.%) to the alloy melt prior to rapid cooling.
generation.conditions: The alloy is processed under identical conditions with an inert atmosphere using rapid cooling techniques (e.g., melt spinning with cooling rates in excess of ~3000 K/s) to obtain an amorphous structure; phosphorus content is maintained as in the baseline alloy.
generation.structural_mediator: Carbon atoms are incorporated interstitially, creating local lattice distortions and increasing melt viscosity that impede atomic mobility and crystal nucleation.
generation.mechanism: The added carbon increases the effective viscosity of the melt and disrupts the short-range atomic ordering necessary for crystallization. This suppression of atomic diffusion delays the onset of crystallization, thereby expanding the stability window of the amorphous phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: The carbon-doped alloy will exhibit a notably higher glass-forming ability, evidenced by a broader supercooled liquid region (an increase in the crystallization onset temperature by ~20 K or more) and a more homogeneous amorphous structure compared to an undoped baseline processed under identical rapid cooling conditions.
generation.baseline: The same phosphorus-containing high‐entropy alloy (e.g., Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20) processed under identical rapid cooling conditions without any carbon addition.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to succeed if the carbon content is maintained within a narrow window (approximately 0.5–2 at.%); it may fail if the cooling rate is insufficient (<1000 K/s) or if excessive carbon leads to secondary phase formation. Moreover, the beneficial effects may be diminished if phosphorus content deviates substantially from the baseline.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties include the precise optimum carbon concentration, potential effects on other mechanical properties (such as ductility), and sensitivity to processing parameters. Variability in melt homogeneity or warming during processing may also affect reproducibility.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy (Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20) doped with approximately 1 at.% carbon and a control set without carbon. Both sets are processed under identical rapid cooling conditions (using melt spinning with cooling rates above ~3000 K/s) under an inert atmosphere. Characterize the resulting microstructures using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Conduct differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to determine the glass transition temperature (Tg) and the crystallization onset temperature (Tx).
measurements: XRD patterns to confirm the extent of amorphization
TEM imaging for atomistic and phase homogeneity
DSC curves to measure Tg and Tx, thereby quantifying the supercooled liquid region (Tx – Tg)
Measurement of critical casting thickness or critical diameter for glass formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant (e.g., >15–20 K) expansion of the supercooled liquid region and/or shows no improvement in amorphous phase fraction or critical diameter compared to the undoped control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The cooling profile recorded during welding (at a cooling rate of 154 K/s) demonstrates that the Cantor alloy solidifies at a temperature of 1478 K []. Previous studies reported its melting temperatures as 1607 K [,], 1523 K [], and 1543 K [], indicating a relatively narrow range of solidification. In contrast, the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy containing phosphorus exhibits a significantly broader solidification temperature range and more complex crystallization behavior. Pronounced thermal effects were observed at T3 = 1291 K and T4 = 1206 K during slow cooling on a copper plate (52 K/s), and at T3 = 977 K and T4 = 960 K during rapid cooling following a brief electric arc pulse (3018 K/s). This marked reduction in solidification temperatures compared to the Cantor alloy demonstrates the role of phosphorus in modifying thermal behavior and promoting amorphization. These results highlight the critical importance of controlling cooling rates and alloy composition to optimize phase stability and microstructure. In this paper, two new high entropy bulk metallic glasses (HE-BMGs) have been successfully fabricated using copper mold casting method, namely Ti20Hf20Cu20Ni20Be20 with a critical diameter of 2 mm and Ti16.7Zr16.7Nb16.7Cu16.7Ni16.7Be16.7 with a critical diameter of 1.5 mm. These two HE-BMGs exhibit high fracture strength over 2300 MPa. The glass forming ability and atomic size distribution characteristics of the HE-BMGs are discussed, and it is found that atomic radius spans over a wide range in HE-BMGs. Moreover, we propose a new parameter δ′ to assess the degree of lattice distortion in high entropy alloys (HEAs). papers.title: Thermal and Structural Analysis of a High-Entropy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 Alloy-Infl
papers.approach: Systematic thermal analysis using variable cooling rates (from slow cooling on a copper plate, to rapid cooling after an electric arc pulse and melt-spinning) to study crystallization and amorphization processes.
papers.findings: Phosphorus addition broadens the solidification temperature range and, under sufficiently high cooling rates, promotes the formation of an amorphous (metallic glass) phase. Specific crystallization temperatures corresponding to various phases were recorded; very rapid cooling resulted in a predominantly amorphous structure as confirmed by XRD and TEM.
papers.mechanism: Phosphorus alters the phase diagram by promoting phosphide or phosphorus‐rich intermediate phases and lowering the solidification temperatures of primary phases; these changes enhance the resistance to crystallization under kinetic (rapid cooling) conditions.

papers.title: Predictive Modeling of High-Entropy Alloys and Amorphous Metallic Alloys Using Machine Learning.
papers.system: Bulk metallic glass systems and high-entropy alloys (general framework applicable to compositionally complex and phosphorus-containing systems)
papers.approach: Machine learning–based feature analysis using thermodynamic parameters (e.g., ΔHmix, ΔSmix) and atomic size mismatch to predict glass-forming ability (GFA) and related mechanical properties.
papers.findings: A more negative enthalpy of mixing and significant atomic size mismatch (enhancing local packing heterogeneity and viscosity) correlate with improved GFA. These studies demonstrate that tuning the energetic and structural parameters can effectively hinder crystal nucleation during rapid cooling.
papers.mechanism: Exothermic mixing increases melt viscosity by lowering atomic mobility thereby favoring glass formation; high configurational entropy reduces the free energy barrier for amorphization.

papers.title: High-entropy induced a glass-to-glass transition in a metallic glass.
papers.system: High-entropy metallic glasses (e.g., NbNiZrTiCo HEMG and its variants)
papers.approach: Thermal treatment/annealing experiments on as-prepared high-energy amorphous states to induce an irreversible glass-to-glass transition.
papers.findings: A controlled heat treatment shifted a high-energy glass state to a thermodynamically more stable low-energy state. This transition was accompanied by a significant exothermic event and improvements in mechanical properties such as higher modulus and hardness.
papers.mechanism: The high-entropy effect raises the energy of the as-prepared glass, and targeted thermal annealing promotes atomic rearrangement that minimizes free energy and enhances thermal stability.

papers.title: Designing High Entropy Bulk Metallic Glass (HE-BMG) by Similar Element Substitution/Addition.
papers.system: High-entropy bulk metallic glasses based on Ti, Zr, Hf, Cu, Ni, Be systems
papers.approach: Substitution and microalloying of similar elements to adjust the atomic size distribution and lattice distortion (quantified by the δ′ parameter) to optimize glass-forming ability.
papers.findings: Alterations in the atomic radius distribution—through similar element substitution/addition—can tune the degree of lattice distortion. A carefully optimized δ′ can favor the formation of an amorphous phase over crystalline phases.
papers.mechanism: Increasing lattice distortion disrupts long-range order by creating dense, irregular atomic packings that impede nucleation of crystals, thus supporting the formation and thermal stabilization of an amorphous phase.

papers.title: Crystalline and amorphous structure selectivity of ignoble high-entropy alloy nanoparticles during laser ablation in organic liquids is set by pulse d
papers.system: Cantor-like high-entropy alloy nanoparticles prepared via laser ablation in organic liquids
papers.approach: Laser ablation with controlled pulse duration and interaction with organic solvents, which introduces active carbon species that can dope the forming nanoparticles.
papers.findings: Amorphous phase formation is promoted when longer laser pulse durations (e.g., ns pulses) are used, likely due to carbon diffusion from the organic medium. This carbon doping appears to elevate the glass-forming ability by stabilizing the disordered structure.
papers.mechanism: The incorporation of carbon into the alloy structure interferes with atomic diffusion and crystallization kinetics, further lowering the effective liquidus temperature and enhancing viscosity, thereby promoting an amorphous state and advanced thermal stability.

established: Phosphorus addition in high-entropy alloys broadens the solidification temperature range and aids in forming an amorphous state under rapid cooling.
High mixing entropy and atomic size mismatch are key factors that enhance the glass-forming ability by hindering atomic mobility and nucleation.
Cooling rate is a critical processing parameter; extremely rapid cooling (e.g., melt spinning) is necessary to achieve amorphous structures in these systems.

approaches_tried.approach: Varying the cooling rate using methods such as slow cooling, electric arc pulse, and melt-spinning.
approaches_tried.outcome: Rapid cooling leads to increased undercooling and successful amorphization, while slower cooling results in multiple crystalline phases.

approaches_tried.approach: Microalloying and similar element substitution (adjusting δ or δ′ parameters) to modify lattice distortion.
approaches_tried.outcome: Tuning the atomic size distribution can favor amorphous phase formation but may simultaneously impact ductility and other mechanical properties.

approaches_tried.approach: Thermal annealing to trigger a glass-to-glass transition.
approaches_tried.outcome: Heat treatment can convert a high-energy, metastable amorphous state to a thermally more stable, low-energy state, improving mechanical properties.

approaches_tried.approach: Laser ablation in organic liquids with attention to pulse duration and consequent carbon incorporation.
approaches_tried.outcome: Longer laser pulses (ns) and the resulting carbon doping promote amorphization and may further stabilize the amorphous structure.

mechanisms: Phosphorus modifies solidification by promoting phosphide-rich intermediate phases and lowering nucleation barriers.
High configurational entropy increases melt viscosity and raises the free energy barrier for crystallization.
Lattice distortion from atomic size mismatch (quantified by δ or δ′) creates a dense, disordered packing that impedes crystal formation.
Carbon incorporation (via doping during laser ablation) interferes with atomic mobility and can depress the liquidus temperature.
disagreements: While phosphorus is shown to enhance glass-forming ability, its impact on mechanical properties such as ductility may be detrimental in some studies.
Some approaches (e.g., microalloying with elements similar in size to main constituents) have little effect on GFA, suggesting that not all microalloying additions are beneficial.
There is debate over whether high-entropy effects always improve GFA, with some evidence indicating that raising the liquidus temperature (by certain substitutions) can instead deteriorate GFA.
open_questions: Can additional minor dopants (beyond phosphorus) be identified that improve both the glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys?
How does the interplay between phosphorus and potential dopants (e.g., carbon or other metalloids) affect the balance between enhanced amorphization and mechanical ductility?
What are the optimum processing conditions (e.g., cooling rate, heat treatment protocols) that maximize both GFA and thermal stability without adverse effects on other material properties?
How standard thermodynamic parameters (such as ΔHmix and δ′) can be further refined to predict improvements in thermal stability specific to phosphorus-containing systems?
opportunities: Investigating a single intervention – such as low-level carbon doping – to be introduced into phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys might further impede atomic mobility, lower the liquidus temperature, and thus enhance both glass-forming ability and thermal stability.
Combining phosphorus addition with targeted microalloying of a dopant that introduces favorable lattice distortion (optimized δ′) represents an opportunity to achieve a more stable amorphous phase.

Systematic studies adjusting processing parameters (e.g., exploring a narrow window of cooling rates and subsequent heat treatments) could elucidate the trade-offs between amorphization and ductility, guiding the design of compositionally optimized alloys.

Applying machine learning models that integrate subtle effects of minor dopants (including carbon) alongside phosphorus could accelerate the discovery of compositions with superior thermal and mechanical performance.

directions.direction: Apply minor carbon doping to phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys
directions.assessment: This intervention directly targets both the glass‐forming ability (GFA) and thermal stability by incorporating carbon interstitially to increase melt viscosity and disrupt atomic rearrangements. It is supported by evidence from laser ablation studies showing that carbon incorporation (via ns pulse processing) can enhance amorphization (see PMC12278108::web::039::conclusion and PMC12278108::web::037::conclusion). Its mechanism is well established and the doping level (around 1 at.%) is feasible without major compositional disruption.

directions.direction: Substitute or microalloy with similarly sized elements to tune lattice distortion (δ′ parameter)
directions.assessment: By altering the atomic size distribution, one can enhance lattice distortion to impede crystallization. Although evidence supports that an optimized δ′ favors amorphous phase formation (PMC8911233::web::012::5_conclusions), the risk of adverse effects on ductility or other properties is higher and the effect is less direct on thermal stability.

directions.direction: Optimize rapid cooling processing conditions (e.g., melt spinning) further
directions.assessment: While higher cooling rates evidently improve amorphization by promoting undercooling, this approach is already well explored in existing studies (see PMC11642357::web::021::5_conclusions) and may not additionally enhance the thermal stability of the already–formed amorphous phase.

directions.direction: Employ controlled post-synthesis thermal annealing to trigger a glass-to-glass transition
directions.assessment: A controlled annealing treatment can transform a high-energy amorphous state into a lower-energy, thermally stable one (PMC9023469::web::019::discussions). However, this requires an extra processing step and does not represent a single-point intervention during synthesis.

directions.direction: Use laser ablation in organic liquids with tuned pulse durations to incorporate carbon
directions.assessment: Laser ablation with longer pulse durations leads to carbon incorporation, which boosts the glass-forming ability as reported (PMC12278108::web::039::conclusion). Although effective, this technique may be less easily scaled to bulk synthesis compared to direct microalloying.

choice.direction: Apply minor carbon doping to phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys
choice.why: Carbon doping is a single compositional intervention that can be integrated into the alloy melt prior to rapid cooling. It is expected to enhance the GFA by increasing melt viscosity and interfering with crystallization kinetics, while also broadening the supercooled liquid region (i.e. improving thermal stability). This approach is supported by evidence from studies where carbon incorporation via controlled processes promoted amorphous phase formation.
